claims: The "No Tax on Tips" policy is implemented via the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
The "No Tax on Tips" policy allows eligible workers in over 70 tipped occupations to deduct up to $25,000 in voluntarily received cash tips from their federal income taxes from 2025–2028.
The deduction excludes automatic gratuities.
The deduction applies to employees in food service, hospitality, and personal services who report their tips.
Workers must be in a "customarily tipped" occupation to be eligible for the "No Tax on Tips" policy.
Customarily tipped occupations include restaurant servers, bartenders, hairdressers, valets, and taxi drivers.
Only voluntary cash tips (including credit card tips) qualify for the deduction.
Automatic service charges for large parties are not included in qualified tips.
The deduction limit is up to $25,000 per tax year.
The deduction benefit phases out for individuals with a modified adjusted gross income over $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers).
Tips must be reported to the employer for payroll tax purposes to qualify for the deduction.
The 2025 standard deduction is $15,750 for individuals.
The 2025 standard deduction is $31,500 for married couples.
Individuals earning less than the standard deduction owe no federal income tax.
The IRS has identified over 70 occupations in sectors such as food/beverage, hospitality, personal services, and entertainment that qualify for the deduction.
The tax deduction for tips is valid for the 2025 through 2028 tax years.
Several states, including Arizona, California, Georgia, and others, have proposed their own versions of "no tax on tips" legislation.
The "No Tax on Tips" policy does not exempt tips from Social Security or Medicare taxes, only federal income tax.
Automatic gratuities are treated as taxable wages.
The deduction is only applicable if the tips are officially reported.
